title: Digit-Square Chain Reaches One
statement:
Start from a positive integer n. Replace it with the sum of the squares of its digits, and repeat. For example, 34 becomes 3² + 4² = 25.

Return true if the chain eventually reaches 1, and false if it never does (it then loops forever without touching 1).

examples.why: 7 → 49 → 97 → 130 → 10 → 1. A single digit other than 1 is not automatically a dead end.
11 → 2 → 4 → 16 → 37 → 58 → 89 → 145 → 42 → 20 → 4, and 4 has been seen before. The chain is stuck in a loop that never hits 1.
1² + 0² + 0² = 1 after one step. Zeros contribute nothing.

hints: The chain either reaches 1 or repeats a number it has already produced. Why can't it grow forever?
Any number with many digits shrinks quickly: a 10-digit number maps to at most 10 · 81 = 810. So the chain soon lives among small numbers and must repeat or hit 1.
Detect the repeat. A set of seen values works. For O(1) memory, run a slow pointer one step at a time and a fast one two steps at a time; they meet inside any loop.

explain.intuition:
The chain cannot grow without bound. A number with d digits maps to at most 81 · d, which is much smaller than the number once d ≥ 4. So after a few steps every value is below about 1000, and in a finite set of values the chain must either reach 1 (and stay there, since 1 → 1) or revisit some value and loop forever. The question becomes: does the chain hit 1 before it repeats?

That is cycle detection on an implicit linked list where next(x) is the digit-square sum. A Set of seen values solves it directly. Floyd's tortoise and hare drops the set: move slow one step and fast two steps each round. If there is a loop, fast laps slow and they meet. Since 1 points to itself, reaching 1 is also a "loop", so after they meet you just check whether the meeting value is 1.
steps: Write next(x): peel digits with x % 10 and Math.floor(x / 10), adding each digit squared.
pitfalls: Capping the loop at some fixed number of steps and guessing false. It may pass by luck, but it is not an argument, and an interviewer will ask why that cap is enough.
Assuming single-digit numbers other than 1 are unhappy. 7 reaches 1.
Starting slow and fast at the same value and checking slow === fast before moving. The loop exits at once and every input looks like a cycle.

complexity.time: O(log n) for the first step, then a bounded number of small steps

solutions.title: Remember every value in a set
solutions.idea: Follow the chain, storing each value. Stop when you hit 1 or a value already in the set.

solutions.title: Floyd's slow and fast pointers
solutions.idea: Treat the chain as a linked list. A pointer moving two steps per round catches one moving one step if there is any loop, and 1 is a loop of length one.

followups: Every unhappy chain ends in the same loop through 4. How could you use that to drop the set without Floyd?
Use cubes of digits instead of squares. Does the chain still always end in a loop? Why?
Where else have you used slow and fast pointers? Compare with finding a loop in a linked list.
